title: Buddhisms Two Truths
speaker: Jason Ruvelson
summary: Meditation in Buddhism is not about achieving a specific state or disconnecting from the world, but rather about developing stability and mindfulness in daily life, allowing one to be present and aware in all aspects of existence. Through practice, this stability can lead to fearlessness, clarity, and a greater understanding of oneself and others. By recognizing our interconnectedness and letting go of conceptual thinking, we can gain a deeper appreciation for the world and develop a more direct experience of reality, leading to relaxation, clarity, and connection with all things.

sentences.text: First I just wanted to give a little background about myself and where these teachings come from.
I formally started practicing Buddhism in 1992, and I was introduced to this practice by Paul and Jenny Warwick, who many of you know from the Bellingham dharma hall.
Currently they're on retreat for about a year.
They were and are students of Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche, who was one of the first people to bring Tibetan Buddhism to the West.
He came here after China invaded Tibet and studied at Oxford.
He really wanted to share these teachings here, and eventually he came to the United States and began teaching.
He taught numerous people.
This community has grown greatly because of him, and we have centers all over the United States and all over the world within this lineage.
This lineage is from Tibet.
It's of the Kagyu and Nyingma tradition, which can be traced all the way back, from teacher to student, to the time of the Buddha.
I say all this because in our community lineage is very important.
There's something about this direct line of teachings coming from student to teacher.
And there's actually something particular about Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche and the trust he had in Western students, that he encouraged them to teach.
He wasn't the only one who taught in our community.
He actually trusted his students, so that they became teachers and we could spread and share the teachings with other people.
So students became teachers, and teachers continued to be students.
After having studied with Paul and Jenny Warwick, I went to Naropa University, as Tim mentioned, and later became a student of Sakyong Mipam Rinpoche.
The Sakyong Mipam Rinpoche is the son of Chogyam Trungpa Rinpoche and the current holder of our lineage, Shambhala.
Today's talk on the two truths, relative and ultimate reality, wasn't the original idea of what I would give a talk on.
It was really "why meditate?"
So the talk is going to begin there: why people are drawn to Buddhism, or for that matter, why they are drawn to meditate.
Why maybe many of you are here today.
It seems like people definitely come for many different reasons.
Some are having a hard time in their lives and they think meditation might help.
They feel really anxious in the world and they have this idea that meditation will help them relax.
Some people might go hear a teacher like the Dalai Lama, who was recently in Vancouver, and feel really inspired and think, well, if I meditate maybe I can be somewhat like him.
Or reading the Dharma, you just become the Dharma.
Dharma means truth.
It is also the teachings of Buddhism.
I just wanted to explain that.
So you might read some books on Dharma, Buddhist teachings, and feel very drawn and become curious and want to meditate.
There are also all kinds of ideas about what meditation is and maybe what it is not.
For instance, I think when people think of the idea of meditating, they think it means, oh well, I am just going to calm down and relax and maybe sit there and bliss out and feel good.
For all of you here who have practiced Buddhism, you realize right away that is not what happens, at least in the beginning.
We sit down and we start practicing and we begin to notice how speedy our minds are and how many thoughts are arising, and it might even feel quite uncomfortable.
So meditating in general, and specifically in our tradition, is not about disconnecting ourselves from the world.
It is not about going in a cave and practicing.
It is not particularly about becoming a monk, although there are quite a few people in our tradition and within Buddhism who are monks.
But I think Buddhism has been reaching a different way of presenting itself here in the West.
In our community sometimes we talk about householder yogis.
So basically it is about becoming a better human being and about being in the world.
About being in our jobs and having a family.
Becoming a better human being, and maybe even more than that, creating enlightened society.
When we practice and we teach Dharma in our community, that is something we are continually looking at.
It is actually a practice of training the mind.
In the beginning, when we practice meditation, what we are doing is developing some kind of stability.
We might also say mindfulness, which is the ability of our mind to be present with some object.
It might be like when we are reading a book, that you are actually able to look at the words, understand what you are reading and not be distracted.
It can be as simple as that.
It is also like when you are cooking a meal, that you stay present and you are actually in the process of cooking.
That you are focused on that.
You are experiencing that.
Maybe even appreciating that.
When you are relating to other people in communication, stability of mind is also related to the ability to listen.
So you can be there with someone and hear what they are saying without planning your next thought or planning what you are going to say to them.
You are actually just able to be there and hear what they are saying.
The Buddha, and long before that, used this practice of sitting meditation, where you sit on the cushion, place your mind on an object and practice cultivating mindfulness.
For us this seemingly simple exercise sometimes can be a little difficult.
In the beginning we ask ourselves to sit down on a cushion on the floor and have our mind stay there in our body and with our breath.
Seeming a simple thing: just to sit down and have our mind sit down with us.
Yet it is not always so simple.
Our mind tends to wander off and think about other things.
It is actually just a reflection of what it is like in the rest of our lives.
Whenever we are trying to be present doing something, how often our mind wanders off to the past or the future, planning ahead and not really just being here.
So I think we should do just a little exercise of practicing together for a minute.
What I would like everyone to do is take a good posture.
In this case, on these few benches, it means maybe sitting forward a tiny bit, or at least not leaning back.
There is some notion of sitting upright, dignified like a king or queen, and relaxed.
Our eyes are open with our gaze slightly lowered to focus.
Our attention is on the breath.
Feeling the texture of the breath, simply being here.
When we notice our minds start to wander, gently come back to the breath.
We are not trying to stop our thoughts from coming.
We are not trying to suppress anything.
Actually we are just letting our natural thoughts and emotions arise.
We touch them, let them go and come back.
Maybe it doesn't sound like much of a big deal, and actually it is not.
Although so much of our habitual tendency is that when we are experiencing something, we tend to get caught up in it.
Especially if it is some kind of painful emotion or something rather exciting, and we get lost.
We end up tripping, literally or metaphorically.
And the more we practice, the more we develop some kind of fearlessness.
Fearlessness that is not tough and hard, but fearlessness that we are not afraid of our own experience.
That we are not afraid of letting the world touch us.
That we don't have to protect ourselves so much.
The more we practice, the more our mind becomes stable, settles down.
Clarity emerges.
We begin to see things a little more clearly.
We begin to see ourselves a little more clearly.
On the cushion, I say cushion because that is where we sit, not cushion, but on the cushion, this clarity appears as almost some kind of space around our thoughts or emotions.
It is like there is some kind of room, and you can see your thoughts arise and see them fall away, or see an emotion building and watch it come and watch it go.
And there becomes some kind of choice in the matter.
We actually have a choice about letting it go.
It is not like some kind of seed of aggression pops up and all of a sudden we are yelling at someone.
And it is so habitual and you don't even have a choice.
You are just caught in some kind of repetitive thought that keeps you awake at night.
So there is some kind of room and we can see what we are doing, whether it is something that is helpful for us or something that is fruitless.
I say that because for so many of us we end up worrying.
Right now at my job it is budget season, and there are so many people worrying about whether they are going to get a raise or not.

There are little comments here and there, and people are projecting all kinds of ideas about whether they are going to get a raise or not going to get a raise, or why they deserve it, or what didn't happen, or what is going on.
Then they start getting all upset because they know they are not going to get it.
And it is all projections.
They still don't really know what is happening, and none of that is really helpful.
Although there may be some pieces of it that might be helpful.
Maybe we can realize what it is that we can do in that situation, with our boss or supervisor, that might illuminate why we deserve a raise.
Or maybe there is nothing we can do, and what we can do is continue doing our job and just relax and wait, and not get sleepless and hope and fear and all this stuff we go crazy about.
I guess I could talk about relationships too.
This almost seems too obvious.
There are so many projections that go on, people getting caught up all the time around hope and fear that has nothing to do with what is going on in front of us.
Meditation is very helpful in these kinds of situations.
It helps us deal with our relative ordinary reality.
We can just become a little more skillful.
We can see ourselves getting caught up in stuff, and maybe we can even just simply let it go.
The more you practice, the more you become familiar with your own patterns.
You start to see the same kind of worries come up, the same kind of concerns, the same kind of intense emotions.
After a while they get a little old.
They get a little tiresome, and you might even want to just give them up.
After a while of seeing them so many times they become just not such a big deal.
So you see worry come up or you see fear come up and you just notice it, touch it, not such a big deal, and you're able to let it go.
Obviously it's not always like this, and this is a practice.
It's a practice both on the cushion and off the cushion.
Relative truth is ordinary reality.
And it's about getting more skillful in dealing with ordinary reality: people around us, our jobs, our relationships and so forth.
The other thing that happens in meditation, and this is kind of a leap, but not such a big leap, is that we may experience some kind of glimpse of emptiness.
Emptiness is a term that they use in Buddhism often, and it may not be the best translation.
In this case, a glimpse of emptiness, or a glimpse of emptiness of self, no self.
This emptiness is talking about the belief in a self that's solid, separate from everyone and permanent.
As we practice more and more, we might begin to doubt some of the beliefs we have about who we are.
We have these ideas like, oh, I'm that kind of person, or I'm this kind of person, and the more we practice, these beliefs may not suit us anymore.
You know, they don't quite encompass all of who we are.
The teachings in Buddhism encourage us to look at this.
Buddhism has two profound skillful means.
One of those is practice, the practice of meditation, and the other is study.
They both impact each other.
We practice meditation and we study about it to understand our own experience.
Without meditation the study is fruitless.
It's all up in your head and there's no actual experience.
And yet practice without study isn't always so helpful either, because we can end up fooling ourselves.
So when I thought about this glimpse of emptiness, the thing that came to mind was an experience that I had years ago, when I was living in Bellingham a prior time.
In 1991 or 92 I was living up on Garden Street.
At the time I was having a really hard time with relationships.

I was feeling really bad, and I don't remember exactly what was going on, but I broke up with someone and was feeling pathetic and a little depressed and down on myself, thinking a lot was going on and trying to figure it out and just really caught up.
I walked outside of my house and I was walking around on the lawn, and I looked up and I noticed this beautiful sunset.
I paused for a moment, and in that moment something happened.
I recognized something.
What I recognized is that it wasn't like there was this poor, pathetic self, Jason, over here and some more beautiful sunset over there.
There was something about who I was.
There was something in me that had the capability of actually experiencing this beautiful sunset and the feelings that went along with it.
So it wasn't just that this beautiful experience was over there, outside of me.
The pathetic thing was here in me, and that's who I was.
That's all I was.
And then there was some kind of relaxing right in that moment, just briefly resting.
It wasn't just blissing out, experiencing this nice beautiful sunset, because my pain wasn't gone either.
There was clearly the situation right in my mind.
There was the pain of what was going on.
And there was this beautiful sunset and warm feeling and this full, rich experience that I can't quite put into words exactly, yet I'm sure for many of you it doesn't sound unfamiliar at all.
This wasn't the first time I'd had some kind of full-blown big experience where I was very present.
But I think what was unique about it is that I recognized it.
And the recognition was some kind of contrast, an extreme contrast between seeing before, where I had this very small mind, just this small me, and rather something larger.

So here's where our question of allegiance comes up: whether we can actually hang out and rest in this open, full, rich experience, or whether we're going to solidify our experience, separate it and make it permanent.
For most of us, including myself, I think that's what we do: we solidify it.
It's too easy to go, "Wow, this is really great."
Maybe you even begin to think about yourself, "Wow, I'm just so big, I'm much bigger and more powerful than I ever thought."
And that's not quite it either.
It's just the other side of the same coin.
It's that same habitual pattern of solidifying experience, turning it into something conceptual rather than just being there.
It's all about connecting thoughts, feelings, whatever's arising.
So these notions of me and self and I are very functional, helpful and obviously believable.
There's some way of orientating our sense perception, our sight and sound, and they keep pointing back to us, to me, to ourself.
That concept isn't always so necessary, whether it's that moment where I was sitting there experiencing the sunset, or, for many people, even in sports.
They talk about peak experience.
It's far beyond that.
Clearly they have a body and there's a person there, like we talk about a person.
They're just fully in the experience at the moment, whether you're skiing down a mountain or making love or whatever it is.
You don't need that continual reflection of yourself to be there.
The problem with solidifying our experience is that it's not how things are.
Our world is very fluid and everything is interconnected.
I think most of us know that on some level, whether it's through a study of physics or something like that, intellectually.
We know everything is interconnected.
And the Buddhist teachings continually ask us to look: what is this sense of me, of self, of I?
Where do I begin and where do I end?
Where is it?
And it's not something that you do once.
You do it over and over again, deepening.
This separate sense of self is part of our survival skills.
I think it's what's kept human beings alive for so many years.
It's related to fight or flight, that ability to want to protect ourselves, to feed ourselves.
I think it's even connected to procreating.
We have this separate sense of self and we really want to have union, so we're continually looking outside of ourselves to find some kind of union with other.
It's built into us, even biologically.
But one of the things that we can recognize about that sense of separateness is that we already are in union.
We already are connected.
That's how things really are.
The Buddhist teachings go even a little bit further when they talk about emptiness.
It's not just emptiness of self.
They also say emptiness of other.
Emptiness sounds like there's not much to say about it, and yet in Buddhism they're talking about emptiness in any other subject.
When they talk about things, phenomena, self and other, reality, it's said that they're beyond the four extremes.
And the four extremes are phenomena.
So that phenomena does not... it's beyond these four extremes.
The extremes being that things exist, that things don't exist, that things both exist and don't exist, or neither existent nor non-existent.
That all sounds kind of heady and out there, but I say this because it's actually what drew me to Buddhism in the first place.
When I met Paul Warwick in '92, I was really into philosophy and curious about ideas and looking at the nature of mind and reality.
In a lot of ways I think I'm just really up in my head.
I started listening to him, and we started talking about emptiness and these four extremes, and I found there was nothing I could hold on to.
There was no idea or thing I could figure out about how things really were, or are.
It began to push me beyond some conceptual understanding.
That's the whole point in Buddhism of what they call Madhyamaka.
These almost intellectual exercises use our minds to push us beyond our mind, conceptual mind, that is.
When we talk about emptiness, it's not just empty.
It's not nihilism.
It's not void.
I think it's one of the traps: that every Buddhism is about emptiness, it's about nothing, and what's the big deal?
Why bother looking at it, and why talk about it?
It's just empty and meaningless, and what's the point?
You're just supposed to sit there and breathe and not do anything.
That's not what we're talking about at all.
From the very beginning we're talking about how to become better human beings.
This point of emptiness is trying to point out that we're caught up in stuff that may not be as solid as we think it is.
As we practice meditation further and further, that glimpse of emptiness is also a glimpse of what in our tradition we call basic goodness, or in traditional Buddhism they talk about Buddha nature.
So it's this experience that's not based on anything.
It's this unflappable quality that no matter what arises, it's always with us and always there.
A couple weeks ago, a student at a weekend training we were having was talking about the Dalai Lama and how he had said something about the depths of the ocean.
The depths of the ocean is also a metaphor for this Buddha nature, or basic goodness, or this quality that we all have.

No matter what's on the surface, little thoughts bubbling or emotions or craziness going on in our lives or hurricanes on the level of the sea, it's all just this natural display and radiance of the depths of the ocean of who we are.
So again, when we talk about emptiness, it's empty of what?
The permanent self, yes.
It's also absence of conceptualization, absence of the ideas, the thoughts we have about something.
For instance, when you look at a bird or an eagle, it's easy just to look and go, "Oh, there's an eagle."
But on some level when we do that, we stop seeing.
All we end up doing is seeing our label.
So our practice in meditation is asking us to go beyond that, to go further into experience, to have the world become richer to us, more alive, more full.
And we actually gain a greater appreciation of how things are, of our own lives.
It's even possible to have a non-conceptual experience of a thought.
Again, we're not trying to get rid of thoughts, and we're not saying thoughts aren't helpful.
It's the stories we get caught up in that just go nowhere, or end up basically not being helpful.
So through meditation what we learn is to relax.
We learn to relax with ourselves.
We learn to relax in our world.
We learn to relax with our own experience.
And the world becomes more alive, more clear, more vivid.
There's this notion of emptiness, but it's not just empty, it's full too.
It's full of form.
It's full of all of us sitting here in this room.
Ultimate reality is that union of both form and emptiness, of relative reality and the nature of things.
The experience of it is like sitting on a razor's edge, sitting on the razor's edge of life, vibrant and awake, in contact with the world.
So I think we'll end here and take a break.
For those of you who want to leave, you're welcome to leave.
And for those of you who want to ask some questions and stay around, that's fine.
Let's get together for a minute.
Ultimate reality is interesting.
One thing about Buddhism in general is that you study something and you eventually gain some understanding about what it is.
Then as time goes on you realize you don't understand, and you go further into it.
I realized even in preparing for this talk that my experience was very alive for me, so it's like, "Oh yeah, of course I can talk about ultimate reality."
Then I get into it more and more, and my own understanding starts to come into question.
One of the things that came up for me in studying it was that we often talk about emptiness as being ultimate reality.
Emptiness, they might say, is dharmakaya.
It's basically a metaphor: the fabric of space, or pregnant space.
So that's dharmakaya.
But when you talk about ultimate reality, you can't talk about it separate from form.
You also can't talk about it separate from relative reality, because it's not like all there is is emptiness and space.
There's also arising.
There's also us here, sitting here.
It's probably not quite as solid as we think it is.
Again, there are different kinds of emptiness.
There's emptiness of self, and there's emptiness of self and other, or emptiness of other.
And dharmakaya, I guess, is speaking to all of that.
But the danger here is intellectualizing this stuff too much, and any time you talk about it, it's hard not to go there.
That's why it's so important to practice.
It isn't some intellectual understanding.
It's an actual experience.
But these teachings help point that out to us, to see when we're fooling ourselves and getting caught, and so on.
Yes, very much.
What to say about that?
It's interesting, because in doing this talk I realized I can't speak for all of Buddhism.
I realized some things are very similar and maybe identical, and other things may be very different.
The one thing that I think is true of all Buddhism is the three jewels of Buddha, Dharma and Sangha.
We value them all equally and profoundly.
The Sangha, being community: we're going to practice together, our community acts as mirrors for us, we support each other, and it illuminates ourselves.
And Dharma teachings, the truth of how things are, but also Buddhist teachings.
There are many kinds of Buddhist teachings.
There are some that are more psychological and some that go further into emptiness, and so on and so on.
And also the notion of Buddha.
Buddha being the historical Buddha, someone who started this lineage and began these teachings.
Buddha also is an inherent nature, Buddha nature, basic goodness.
It's something within ourselves, all of us.
The historical Buddha was a human being, just like us, and exemplified that same potential that we have.
Sorry, I expanded on Sangha a little bit.
Actually, more about Sangha: it's fun to practice together.
It's one of the great things about here in Bellingham.
We have this Dharma hall and people come together and practice.
I know in our group we definitely have fun practicing together and having tea and chatting and studying together.
I'm sure the same is true in other groups.
That's a big part of Buddhism in general.
Other questions?

**Participant:** The Sangha refers to the community of the enlightened. [unclear: "To say you're arhats and make sense."] If you're talking about the three jewels and they're kind of the equivalent of what Buddha in the general community can be very confused.
So to inflate it as a jewel might be a little misleading.
And then to have some understanding that the Sangha actually refers to...
**Jason Ruvelson:** Again, I think Sangha is spoken on different levels.
Sure, Sangha could be those enlightened beings that have gone before us.
They're part of the lineage that brought the teachings here to us.
They're also our local community of people that practice together, that support us in our own practice.
And I also think they could be considered all human beings on the planet, for that matter all beings in the universe, seen and unseen.
If you say Sangha by definition is those enlightened beings, well, that's something we all have, by nature.
Maybe it's not recognized right now.
So I think to pin Sangha down to one group and not another...
**Participant:** Indra's net?
**Jason Ruvelson:** What did you say?
**Participant:** Is that what Trungpa Rinpoche?
